scenes.title: The avoidance loop
scenes.sub: Triggers · what the fantasy pays out · the loop, link by link
scenes.say: Chapter three. The loop that turns uncomfortable work into lost sessions.
A recall from chapter two. According to the coping lens, what does the fantasy do for you?
scenes.sayA: It repairs your mood in the moment, through escape, wish fulfilment and soothing. But it predicts more distress later.
scenes.a: Repairs mood now; predicts more distress later

scenes.head: How to read the evidence in this chapter
items: Experiments show cause, but mostly in the general population
Diaries and long-term studies show what follows what
Surveys and interviews show links and lived experience
scenes.say: MD research rarely runs experiments, so watch the labels in this chapter. Experiments show cause, but nearly all of them come from the general population. Diaries and long-term studies show what follows what, which is stronger than a correlation, but not proof. Surveys and interviews show links and lived experience.

scenes.head: What starts an episode
items: Music: common, but best seen as an amplifier
scenes.say: The proposed criteria list the best-supported triggers: music, repetitive movement, distress or boredom, and being alone. Movement went with fantasy in 79 percent of one sample, and one diary participant said running, walking and driving trigger daydreams better than sitting still. Solitude is close to a precondition. During Italy's COVID lockdown, 17 percent of 6,277 adults screened as probable MD. And strong emotion, of either kind, pulls thought into fantasy.

scenes.by: Forum post, cited by Burrell et al. 2025
scenes.text: My brain has sort of been trained to escape into daydreams whenever I'm *stressed, bored, or overwhelmed*.
scenes.note: Fantasising to regulate emotion can become a habit
scenes.say: Researchers call this affective salience. Strong emotion pulls on thought, and the pleasure of emotional gratification grabs attention automatically. One forum post puts it plainly: my brain has sort of been trained to escape into daydreams whenever I'm stressed, bored, or overwhelmed. Over time, fantasising to regulate emotion can become habitual.

scenes.text: In diaries, a bad mood one day did *not* predict more MD the next day. Distress probably acts within ~minutes or hours~, and nobody has measured that yet.
scenes.say: There is a timing wrinkle. In a 14-day diary study, low mood or anxiety on one day did not predict more MD the next day, and over 13 months, distress did not predict later MD either. Both teams suggest distress acts within minutes or hours, which day-level studies cannot see. Nobody has yet measured the minute-by-minute sequence of a hard task, then discomfort, then an episode.

scenes.head: The fantasy pays out twice

items: Power and dominance, for grandiose types
Relief from stress, shame, low self-worth

scenes.say: MD is rewarding in two ways at once. It adds pleasure: romance, celebrity, wish fulfilment and an idealised version of yourself. Among 539 probable sufferers, people high in grandiosity used fantasy for power and dominance. And it removes pain: it soothes distress and loneliness, escapes boredom, and relieves stress, shame and low self-worth. Among 242 sufferers, sensitivity to reward was the most prominent trait.

scenes.head: Discomfort intolerance
scenes.text: People with MD show *higher frustration intolerance* and more avoidance coping. Discomfort intolerance ‘should be of ~significant focus~ in MD therapy’.
scenes.note: This is your pattern: it starts when the work gets uncomfortable
scenes.say: One finding fits your pattern especially closely. In a study of 317 people, those with MD had higher frustration intolerance and more avoidance-based coping. The authors concluded that discomfort intolerance should be of significant focus in MD therapy. That is your pattern: it starts when the work gets uncomfortable. People with MD also avoid unpleasant inner experiences more, and judge themselves more harshly.

scenes.text: In the moment, more MD went with *less* depression and anxiety. But it ~cannot be considered an effective emotion regulation strategy~.
scenes.say: The relief is real in the moment. Within one group of 252 people with MD, more daydreaming went with less depression and anxiety, which the authors read as MD managing emotion. But the meta-analysis authors' overall verdict is that it cannot be considered an effective emotion regulation strategy. Here is why.

scenes.head: The loop, link by link
scenes.say: Here is the whole loop. One: work gets hard, boring or uncertain. Two: the unpleasant feeling becomes an urge to escape. Three: the music goes on, and immersion deepens. Four: instant relief, pleasure, and a sense of competence. Five: that relief strengthens the habit, so the urge comes faster next time. Six: hours are lost, and the work goes undone. Seven: guilt, shame, and a widening gap between fantasy and reality. Eight: more negative emotion the next day. And nine: the lower mood feeds the next urge.

scenes.head: The strongest links are experiments
items: costs go to your future self
Believe your mood is ‘frozen’: procrastination vanishes
scenes.say: The general-population links are the most solid. A meta-analysis of 691 correlations found that how unpleasant a task feels is one of the strongest predictors of procrastination. Researchers describe procrastination as short-term mood repair, with the costs borne by the future self. And the causal test is striking: when people were led to believe their bad mood was frozen and could not be changed, their procrastination disappeared.

scenes.text: People put off work *because they expect the escape to make them feel better*.
scenes.note: Induced low mood also caused more lapses and off-task thoughts
scenes.say: In other words, people put off work because they expect the escape to make them feel better. A second experiment found that putting people in a low mood made them lapse more, report more off-task thoughts, and become less inclined to re-engage after a lapse.

scenes.head: The day after a high-MD day (diaries, 77 people)
scenes.say: The MD-specific evidence covers the back half of the loop. In the diaries, a day with more MD was followed the next day by more negative emotion, more dissociation, and more obsessive compulsive symptoms. The authors concluded that in the long term, MD does not bring pleasure, but distress.

scenes.text: MD predicted later *stress, anxiety and depression*. Distress did ~not~ predict later MD.
scenes.note: ‘Escape in the short term that results in long-term impairment’
scenes.say: Over 13 months, in 814 people, MD predicted later stress, anxiety and depression. But distress did not predict later MD. The authors put it simply: MD may be used to escape distress in the short term, and it results in long-term impairment.

scenes.text: The *widening gap* between the idealized fantasy and reality, a disillusionment that is often ~eased with further daydreaming~.
scenes.say: Researchers describe how the loop closes. MD creates more distress from the time wasted, and from the widening gap between the idealised fantasy and reality, a disillusionment that is often eased with further daydreaming. One published case, a 25-year-old man, showed the online version: escapist activities caused impairment, which led to more daydreaming and more internet use to relieve the distress.

scenes.head: Your lever
scenes.text: The escape runs on a *belief*: that it will repair your mood. The evidence: MD is followed by a ~worse~ mood the next day.
scenes.note: When the urge hits: the relief is borrowed from tomorrow
scenes.say: This gives you a practical lever. The escape is driven by the belief that it will repair your mood. But the evidence shows MD is followed by a worse mood the next day. Next time the urge hits, remember that the relief is borrowed from tomorrow.
In the Tice experiment, what made procrastination disappear?
scenes.sayA: Believing their bad mood was frozen and could not be changed. If escape cannot repair your mood, the urge to escape loses its point.
scenes.a: Believing their mood was ‘frozen’, so escape couldn't repair it

scenes.say: Where in the loop does music come in, and what does it do?
scenes.sayA: Link three, right after the urge. It deepens the immersion, and makes the daydream harder to leave.
scenes.a: Link 3, after the urge: it deepens immersion and makes leaving harder

scenes.text: Next: the *bill*. Lost hours, weaker focus, mood a year on, and the special cost of ~success fantasies~.
scenes.say: Next: the bill. Lost hours, weaker focus, mood a year on, and the special cost of success fantasies.
